newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Renault says can rival best in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Renault says can rival best in Europe.

text.p: French carmaker Renault's reorganisation of its car assembly operations, including the painful decision to close a plant in Belgium, will put the company on a firm footing in Europe to rival the best of its competitors, chairman Louis Schweitzer said on Tuesday.
He said the decision to close the Vilvoorde plant was "a weighty and painful" decision, but the move was necessary and the company preferred to tell the people affected the truth from the start.

"It's a major trauma," he told reporters at the Geneva car show. He said the factors that led to the closure of the Belgian plant were its small size, its limited growth potential -- as it is located in an urban area -- and the need for big investments in the near future in its painting operations to meet European environmental standards.

Schweitzer said he was not surprised by the outcry. "It seems normal to me that a decision of this nature provoke a shock. If we had the feeling that the decision had not been necessary we would not have taken it," he said.
"It's a decision to concentrate industrial production going beyond the plant closure and that was not contingent on negotiation. There was no room for negotiation on the decision itself," he said.
"It seemed preferrable not to mask the reality from the start, not to enter into a game in which we would pretend to be negotiating when the outcome was known," Schweitzer said.
The Vilvoorde site produced just over 140,000 vehicles last year, well below the norm for its competitors, he said.
As a result of the reorganisation Renault will produce cars in fewer sites and lower its costs. Schweitzer put the savings at 850 million francs a year.
"From here to the year 2000, Renault's industrial plant will be competitive, flexible and capable of the best industrial performance that can be found in Europe."

Schweitzer said he was planning to meet representatives of the Belgian workers soon to manage the closure as smoothly as possible. He did not say when or where. "It would be a bit provocative to go to the site," he said.

Schweitzer said the company was seeking a buyer for Vilvoorde, in the same way it was also seeking a partner for the Setubal plant in Portugal. He said the Vilvoorde sale would be made "for a symbolic sum".
Renault also plans to announce an acceleration of its French job cuts plan resulting in some 2,700 cuts for 1997, nearly double the last year's. The plan aims to avoid outright layoffs.
"In a European market where growth prospects are modest, productivity gains must be in excess of volume growth. That inevitably leads to a regular reduction of staff," he said.
"If we want to ensure the future of the company, we can't renounce the possibility of substantial cost reductions," he said.

"In a fiercely competitive climate Renault has managed to increase its market share in January and February from year earlier levels, helped by prior cost reduction efforts and a more aggressive sales policy," Schweitzer said.
But the fact was that the French market was down and prices were not recovering, he said.
The French job cut programme will result in a charge on the 1996 results which will be announced on March 20. Renault has already cautioned that it will show a significant operating loss.
